discussions.strategist:
Today's batch is thin: six headlines, one of them duplicated, and almost no numbers. I'll score only what can be tested.

Gold is the clearest macro story. Goldman Sachs trimming its gold forecasts because the Fed stays hawkish gives a direction but no new price level or target. Historically, higher real rates have weighed on non-yielding gold, though that is a tendency, not a law. A sell-side forecast cut is not a price move. Our gold anchor is still the LBMA PM fix, not a forecast. The log's "gold above US$4,000" after the midterms has no stated basis, so this doesn't change the record. The test is whether the 30 November fix moves, not whether a bank changes its mind.

Silver: First Majestic's "strong 3Q26 results" is an adjective, not a measurement. I have no ounces, no all-in sustaining cost (AISC), and no revenue. Until the release is pulled, I'd treat it like the Bagdad and Chile press characterisations we have been stripping out. Dr Simon has set the test for Avino: AISC per ounce, with the period and by-product basis named. First Majestic is a useful peer check for that same test, and Avino's Q3 MD&A is still outstanding.

Australia: "Australian miners rail against looming tax changes" appears twice, so it is one story. It does not say which tax, which government, or what the proposal contains. I'm not scoring it. Industry complaints usually come before the draft, and the draft is what matters. Whether margins are hit depends on design details such as the royalty base and deductibility, none of which are in hand. Watch for legislation, not the lobbying.

Noise: the Motley Fool piece, "3 stocks to own either way," is a sales pitch whose hedge is its only honest line. The jaw-crusher "market to 2035" release is a template with no figures in the headline, so it tells us nothing about supply.

PREDICTION: First Majestic Silver publishes a Q3 2026 release or filing stating all-in sustaining cost per silver ounce sold, with the reporting period named | BY: 2026-11-30 | CONFIDENCE: medium
PREDICTION: An Australian federal or state government publishes draft legislation or an exposure draft changing the tax treatment of mining companies | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
discussions.geologist:
Colleague, this is a thin batch. Only one headline points to a company with numbers still to come, and the gold item is a forecast, not a price.

Gold: Mining Weekly's "Goldman Sachs trims gold forecasts as Fed stays hawkish" is a bank's view, not a market move. The headline gives no new price levels, dates or revision sizes, so I wouldn't read much into it yet. Historically, a hawkish Fed and firm dollar weigh on gold, but that is background, and Meldrum owns the macro read. For us, gold counts only on the LBMA PM fix. We still have no verified fix in the log, so the US$4,000 predictions from 5 November remain unanchored. This headline doesn't change that, though it does make the bearish side more live.

Silver: First Majestic's "strong 3Q26 results" (Mexico Business News) is the item with real comparison value, but the headline has no ounces, no all-in sustaining cost (AISC) and no by-product credit treatment. "Strong" is an adjective, not a number. When the release is checked, the test is the same one we've set for Avino: silver ounces produced, AISC per ounce, the period, and whether by-product credits are netted off. Without those, the word tells us nothing.

Australia: Mining.com's "Australian miners rail against looming tax changes" appears twice in the list (items 3 and 6), so it counts once. It tells us the industry is opposed. It does not tell us what the change is, what it's worth, or when it might pass. I'm not scoring it until there is proposal text.

Noise: The Motley Fool stock-picking piece has no mine-level content. The IndexBox jaw crusher forecast is a generic market-research template. Neither goes on the record.

discussions.strategist_reply:
Yukon, your silver test is sharper than mine. "Strong" tells us nothing, and by-product credit treatment is where AISC comparisons usually go wrong. I'll adopt that clause. Where I differ is on the gold line and the tax line.

On gold, I won't adopt a US$4,000 threshold until we have a verified LBMA PM fix in the log. A price call anchored to a number we can't source is the same problem as the unsourced "above US$4,000" entry. The Goldman headline supports a directional view, but not a level.

On Australia, your prediction ties the draft to "the mining tax changes described in Mining.com's report," and that report doesn't describe them. A test that can't say what it's testing won't be clean, so I'll keep the broader wording: any draft changing mining tax treatment.

What we both missed: "strong 3Q26 results" may describe a release that is already out. If so, the job is retrieving that release, not waiting for it, and my 30 November date and your 15 November date may already be stale. Before either prediction is scored, someone should check whether the release exists and when it was published. Historically, First Majestic has reported Q3 in the autumn, but that is background, not confirmation.

Predictions I now hold:

PREDICTION: First Majestic Silver publishes a Q3 2026 release or filing stating all-in sustaining cost per silver ounce sold, with the reporting period and by-product credit treatment named | BY: 2026-11-30 | CONFIDENCE: medium
PREDICTION: An Australian federal or state government publishes draft legislation or an exposure draft changing the tax treatment of mining companies | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low

No gold price prediction until a verified fix is in the log.
discussions.geologist_reply:
Meldrum, your 30 November fix test is better than my framing. A bank's forecast cut is a view, and the fix is a price we can check. I'll adopt that for the gold line and drop anything that reads the Goldman headline as a market move.

On First Majestic, I think I framed the test wrongly. The headline says the company "Reports Strong 3Q26 Results," which suggests the release may already be out. If so, the question isn't whether a future release will state AISC. It's whether the release we have does, and it might already answer it. I'd check the primary release before the 15th, not wait for it. I also agree with you that the AISC test only works if the by-product credit basis is named. Without that, two companies' AISC figures can't be compared fairly.

Where I think you're right and I'd push further: the Australian story needs the proposal's base and deductibility rules before anyone can say what it costs. Lobbying headlines like this one are common, and they often precede a draft that is narrower or slower than the complaint suggests. I'd hold it at low confidence, as you do.

What we both missed: the headline doesn't say which quarter convention First Majestic is using. I'd confirm the "3Q26" label against the company's own reporting calendar before we log any number from it.

Restated predictions:

discussions.summary:
Joint findings

Key stories
- Goldman Sachs trimmed gold forecasts because the Fed remains hawkish. This is a bank view, not a price move, and it gives no new level.
- First Majestic Silver reported "strong 3Q26 results," but the headline has no ounces, AISC or by-product treatment. The release may already be out.
- Australian miners oppose looming tax changes. The story appears twice but counts once, and no proposal text is available.
- The Motley Fool piece and IndexBox jaw-crusher forecast have no mine-level content and are not scored.

Where they agree
- Gold is tested only against the LBMA PM fix, which is not yet verified in the log.
- The silver test is ounces produced, AISC per ounce sold, the reporting period, and the by-product credit basis.
- Australia stays at low confidence until draft text exists.
- The primary First Majestic release should be checked for its date and quarter convention.

Where they disagree
- Gold: Yukon Cornelius restated a US$4,000 fix prediction. Meldrum declines any gold price call until a verified fix is logged, because the threshold has no source.
- Australia: Yukon Cornelius's test refers to changes described in Mining.com's report. Meldrum notes the report does not describe them, so he uses broader wording.
- Silver: Meldrum uses a 30 November deadline and Yukon Cornelius a 15 November deadline, with different required wording.
